title: India Warns Border Peace Is Critical to China Ties Amid Arunachal Tensions
excerpt: New Delhi says the state of border affairs will shape broader bilateral relations, as reports emerge of Chinese troops entering Indian-controlled territory near Taksing in Arunachal Pradesh.
body:
• India's foreign ministry stressed border peace is critical to bilateral ties after reports of Chinese patrols 2.5 km inside Indian-controlled territory
  • Chinese troops reportedly pitched tents in the disputed area in early August after a late July face-off near Taksing
  • China says the border situation is "generally stable" and both sides agreed to maintain communications
  • Tensions come ahead of a BRICS summit in New Delhi in September that Xi Jinping is expected to attend

India's foreign ministry said Tuesday that peace along its disputed border with China is critical to the broader bilateral relationship, amid reports of renewed military tensions in a remote corner of the Himalayas.

The statement marks New Delhi's second comment on border matters in less than a week and comes as the two Asian powers attempt to rebuild ties strained by deadly clashes in 2020. It also arrives ahead of a BRICS summit in New Delhi from September 12 to 13 that Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to attend.

"We have always emphasised in discussions with the Chinese side that we consider these issues as most serious. The state of the border affairs will reflect on the state of our larger bilateral ties."

— Randhir Jaiswal, Indian Foreign Ministry Spokesperson

Face-Off Near Taksing

Indian news website ThePrint reported after Tuesday's briefing that Indian and Chinese army patrols came face to face in late July near Taksing, a remote border village in Arunachal Pradesh's Upper Subansiri district bordering Tibet.

The incident reportedly took place 2.5 km inside territory controlled by India in the eastern Himalayas. The Chinese patrol later withdrew, but in early August, Chinese troops returned to the area and pitched a couple of tents, according to the report.

A July 26 letter from a local residents' welfare body to authorities, seen by Reuters, said Chinese personnel were rapidly expanding their presence by "occupying new and important places of our land situated at border area."

China claims Arunachal Pradesh, which it calls Zangnan, as part of southern Tibet. India says the state is an integral and inalienable part of its territory.

Both Sides Seek to Downplay Tensions

The Chinese foreign ministry responded by saying the border situation was "generally stable." Beijing said the two countries had agreed to "maintain communications through diplomatic and military channels and jointly safeguard peace and tranquility in the border areas" at the latest meeting of their joint border affairs consultation panel held in New Delhi last week.

An Indian defence spokesperson for Arunachal Pradesh also dismissed the reports as "unsubstantiated and uncorroborated."

It is not unusual for military patrols of the two countries to confront each other along the 3,488-km frontier, but neither is it a frequent occurrence, according to Reuters.

A History of Border Standoffs

The most significant recent incident came in 2020, when clashes in the western Himalayas killed 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese troops — the first deadly border confrontation between the nuclear-armed neighbors in decades.

Both sides amassed tens of thousands of troops along the frontier until Xi and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi held talks in 2024 and agreed to end the standoff. Since then, both countries have worked to gradually normalize relations, though the border remains heavily militarized.

BRICS Summit Looms Large

The latest tensions carry added significance given the upcoming BRICS summit in New Delhi. Xi's expected attendance would mark a high-profile engagement with India, and any border friction could complicate the diplomatic optics for both governments.

India has consistently maintained that border stability is a prerequisite for normalization of ties. The 2020 clashes disrupted trade, diplomatic exchanges, and bilateral investment, and full restoration has been gradual.

For the Indian diaspora, the India-China relationship has direct implications for regional stability, defense spending priorities, and the broader geopolitical landscape shaping India's economic trajectory and its standing in multilateral forums like BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation.
